newsitem.title: INDIA: India telecom regulators promise fair competition.
newsitem.headline: India telecom regulators promise fair competition.

text.p: Indian telecommunications regulators vowed on Tuesday to ensure fair competition as they took on the task of overseeing a market that has been dominated for decades by a state monopoly.

The three-member Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) told a news conference that they would seek to ensure their independence from the government, which opened up the sector to private firms under an economic reform programme launched in 1991.
Retired high court judge S.S.Sodhi was named the chairman and B.K. Zutshi vice-chairman of the authority, whose third member is N.S. Ramachandran. The regulators assumed office on Tuesday.
"Ensuring competition will be the first priority," Sodhi told Reuters after the news conference.

Private firms, in which a foreign stake of up to 49 percent is allowed, have still to start work on basic telephone services, in which the state-run Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has enjoyed a monopoly for decades.
"Like all other incumbent monopolies they are not likely to make things easy for their competition," independent telecommunications consultant Mahesh Uppal told Reuters.
Many of the private firms that led in a global tender are in the process of going through licensing and financing formalities after being awarded 15-year licences.

A government statement said the regulatory authority will have the powers to recommend the entry of new service providers, ensure technical compatibility and effective connectivity between service providers.
It would also advise the federal government on the industry, fix telecommunication tariffs and monitor the quality of services and protect consumer interests, the statement said.
India says it needs investments of around $60 billion to match countries like Brazil and Malaysia, which have six lines per 100 citizens, compared with India's one line for 100 citizens.
Mobile telephone networks run by private companies are in operation in several Indian cities.

Zutshi is a retired government official with negotiating experience in world trade talks. Ramachandran retired recently as the chairman of the state-run telephone company, Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd (MTNL).
Asked if the regulators nominated by the government would be close to state-run phone departments, Zutshi said: "That perception we will be able to change quickly."
One of the first issues the regulators are expected to deal with is a dispute involving charges for telephone calls made from fixed to mobile networks.
The state-run DoT recently hiked charges for calls made from fixed to cellular networks, which invited protests and a court case from private mobile telephone companies.
